title: Safety Inspection Patterns
body: Every serious finding at ADW over the last two years traces back to the same handful of gaps — missing signage, weak supervision, and dust killing visibility — and they keep costing us tipping errors, exclusion-zone breaches, and near-misses at the same handful of locations. When we treat each one as a one-off instead of a pattern, the same failure just shows up again three months later wearing a different NCR number.
keyPoints: ROM pad is the highest-stakes location on site — it shows up in the SIF inspection, two major NCRs (DT-277 wrong-tipping, ZR-24 exclusion breach), and every monthly inspection. Unlabelled stockpile fingers plus high-grade material plus a history of wrong-tipping is a compounding risk, not three separate issues.

Supervision quality, not equipment or procedure, is the named root cause on the big NCRs. Proposed fixes are almost always supervisory (retraining, monitoring protocols) — track supervisor presence at ROM pad and switchbacks like a KPI, not an afterthought.

Switchbacks 1, 2, and 3 are structural repeat offenders because of ramp geometry — don't wait for a new finding there, assume the exposure is standing and check delineators and center-beam visibility every shift.

Supply-chain shortages (delineators, dust chemical, speed signage) show up disguised as safety findings. If a corrective action closes out as "unavailability of X," that's a procurement escalation, not a closed loop.
Incidents cluster at shift-end, handover, and pre-dawn — the thinnest supervision windows. Extra attention at those times pays off disproportionately.
apply: Walk the ROM pad fingers and check they're still labelled and demarcated — that single gap has already produced two major NCRs (DT-277, ZR-24), both tied to dust cutting visibility right at that spot.
